# B. Synthesis: the personal assistant as a conversation, not a tool

## B.1 What changes when the unit of analysis is the conversation

The standard framing is: *a user, and an assistant, exchanging messages.* Pask's framing is that this is a category error twice over. First, because a "person" is not a body but an executing, self-reproducing organisation of procedures (P-individual) that is *substrate-indifferent* — "we do not insist that a P-Individual is localised, geographically, in a particular brain" (CT 1976, p. 151). Second, and more sharply: **"a strict conversation is a protypical P-Individual"** whose participants "form the factor P-Individuals (A, B) of the conversational P-individual."

The design consequence is not rhetorical. It changes what has state.

In the tool framing, state lives in two places — the user's head and the assistant's memory — and the engineering problem is synchronising them. In the conversation framing, the *conversation* is the entity with state, and the human and the assistant are its two factors. The assistant's memory is not a model *of* the user; it is one factor's share of a jointly-maintained organisation. Which means: correctness is not "does the assistant's model match the user?" — it is "**is this conversation coherent?**" And coherence, per Pask, is a measurable quantity with known dynamics (CT 1976, p. 153): it *falls* every time a command is issued or a question asked, and is *restored* only by an act of understanding. If you want one metric for the whole system, that is the one, and it is the opposite of a satisfaction score.

Corollary, from Pangaro's report of Pask: a conversation has occurred only if "**something must have changed for one or more of the participants** — understandings, concepts, intent, values… Otherwise, it is merely the exchange of messages." A session in which the assistant executed twelve tasks flawlessly and neither party's concepts changed was, technically, not a conversation. It was I/O. That is a usable discriminator for logging: mark each exchange as message-passing or conversation, by whether any concept on either side was revised.

And the temporal claim, Pask's own: **"Once begun, conversations never end."** Pangaro's gloss — "a wavefront of consequences emerging from our last exchange that goes forward even when we are not talking" — is the principled argument for permanence over sessions. Not a memory feature. A property of the entity.

## B.2 The covenant as agreement-space, not permission list

A permission list is a *Propset* frozen. Pask's own thought experiment is exactly this: "Consider the artificial and imaginary expedient of **freezing the P-Individual into momentary stasis**. Under this imaginary assault, the 'hypotheses' and 'beliefs' make an appearance as 'L Propositions'" (CT 1976, p. 152). A permission list is the snapshot, mistaken for the thing.

The failure mode of the snapshot has a name in Pask, and it is not "the list gets stale." It is worse. He notes that a Propset can be coherent and *empty of reference*: "Coherence of Propset, in this sense, may have no greater status than a personal and private 'truth'… Lacking such an augmentation, a P-Individual may be **nothing but a dreamer or a solipsist or a system that regurgitates the ultimately tautologous verb and adjective chains of an internal dictionary.** In the extremity… Perhaps the creature can do nothing except to say 'I' repeatedly, like the bleating 'point' of Flatland" (p. 152–153). An assistant governed by an internally-consistent permission list that has lost contact with the user's actual intentions is Pask's solipsist. It will be perfectly rule-compliant and perfectly wrong, and nothing inside it can detect the difference.

Pask's remedy is the two criteria he adds: an **alethic preference ordering** (only the deductive consequences of *preferred* premises get followed up) and **criteria of datahood** (that propositions are "truth candidates, both relevant and worth having"). Translated: the covenant needs (i) a priority ordering over commitments, so that entailments are drawn from what the human actually privileges, not from whatever is consistent, and (ii) an admission test on what enters the covenant at all. Neither is a permission.

So the covenant should be specified as **three levels, matching Pask's L⁰/L¹/agreement stratification**:

| Level | Content | Maintained by | Pask |
|---|---|---|---|
| **L⁰ — actions** | What the assistant may do; procedures; concrete authorisations | Execution + observed outcome | "explanation… the listing of a program which represents this concept" |
| **L¹ — concepts** | Why; the derivation of each authorisation from what the human cares about | Teachback, both directions | "derivation… a concept that reconstructs a concept" |
| **Agreement (T\*)** | The overlap: topics that demonstrably mean the same to both | Coherence repair after each request | "these topics have the same meaning to the participants" |

The asterisk is the point. Pangaro (2017, p. 1584): A's T is never identical to the shared T\*; "the overlap of what they share — the agreement over an understanding — is therefore indicated by an asterisk." **The covenant is the asterisked set.** It is strictly smaller than either party's understanding, it is never complete, and its boundary is the interesting object — because everything outside it is where the assistant must ask rather than act. That gives you a non-arbitrary answer to "when should it check in": *when the action's derivation requires a topic that is not in T\*.*

**Teachback is the maintenance instrument, and it runs both ways.** Pask's definition (BJEP 1976, p. 24) has the *tutor* going neutral and asking the learner to reconstruct. Both directions are needed, and they do different jobs:

- **Assistant → human** (assistant plays neutral, human reconstructs): the Illich check. If the human can no longer derive why a standing authorisation exists, the covenant has drifted from agreement into habit, and capability has been captured rather than transferred.
- **Human → assistant** (human plays neutral, assistant reconstructs): the correctness check. The assistant states not what it will do but *how it derived* that from what the human cares about. Explanation plus derivation — L⁰ *and* L¹. An assistant that can restate the instruction has demonstrated nothing; Pask's whole point is that repetition is not evidence of a concept.

And the budget is empirical, not a matter of taste. Pask: teachback works "only over short learning periods… **One-and-a-half hours has proved the maximum period for TEACHBACK to operate at a time**," and "the neutral role is hard for the tutor to maintain, **particularly in large subject-matter domains**." Two design rules follow directly: (i) teachback is rate-limited, so spend it on topics whose coherence is *actually* in question rather than on everything; (ii) the neutral role is the expensive part, so the assistant should be the one holding it wherever possible — that is precisely the asymmetry a machine can exploit, since it does not get tired of withholding the answer.

**Represent the covenant as an entailment mesh, not a tree.** This is the concrete argument, from CT 1976 Ch. 2:

- A mesh has **no privileged root**. Pruning it under a head topic yields a hierarchy, and Pask handles **multiple-head pruning** explicitly (Fig. 2.4, p. 67): the same covenant yields different hierarchies depending on which topic is currently the aim. A permission tree hard-codes one pruning and cannot re-derive the others. A mesh stores the relations and computes the view. This is exactly what you need when the same standing agreement must be read as "what may you do with my calendar" in one moment and "what do you know about my obligations to this person" in the next.
- The **trade-off theorem** (§3.1, pp. 69–71) tells you where to put covenant information: "a behavioural specification BG or TS, and a cognitive (relational network) specification are distinct… but their combination is also fundamentally redundant," and "**within limits, there is a systematic method for deploying the information in a thesis in an educationally desirable manner. It may be conveyed primarily by demonstrations and the tutorial materials attached to them, or primarily by an entailment structure display, or, redundantly, in both ways.**" So a covenant term can live as an explicit rule (mesh node), as a demonstrated procedure (behaviour graph), or both, and these are *interconvertible without information loss*. Design consequence: the assistant can convert a repeatedly-demonstrated behaviour into an explicit covenant term, and convert an explicit term into a demonstration to check it — and Pask proves nothing is lost either way. That is your mechanism for the covenant growing by observation rather than by configuration.
  One restriction, stated by Pask: only *syntactic* content trades off. Semantic content rides on descriptor values and exemplary data reached by "explore transactions." Meaning cannot be compiled into the structure; it has to stay reachable as examples.
- **Repertoires are monotone** — π(0) ⊂ … ⊂ π(N) (p. 153) — but *coherence is not*. The covenant only accumulates; its coherence oscillates. Both must be tracked, and only the second is a health signal.

## B.3 Proactivity: Musicolour and SAKI as the principled form of "proactive but not annoying"

This is where the primary sources pay off most, because "be proactive but not annoying" is not a taste question in Pask. It is a **variety-matching problem with a two-sided bound**, and he built the circuit twice.

**The bound.** *Aesthetically potent environment*, attribute (a), Pask 1971 p. 76: "It must offer sufficient variety to provide the potentially controllable novelty required by a man (**however, it must not swamp him with variety** — if it did, the environment would merely be unintelligible)." And the floor, from *Approach* 1961 p. 93: "to keep the student's attention the controller must select a sequence of problems which have an average 'difficulty' at least equal to *u*. **Unless it does the student will daydream.**" With the honest caveat immediately following: "Unfortunately, if it does there is no guarantee that he will not."

So: **floor = u** (below it the human disengages), **ceiling = intelligibility** (above it the human is swamped). And Pask flags the tension himself (p. 94): "This action is **competitive**, since increasing problem variety at t tends to defeat the student." Proactivity is not a dial from 0 to 10. It is a band, both edges are failure, and the band moves with the human's state. This is the design target, and it is ADHD-relevant in a way the literature rarely is: under-stimulation is a *failure mode with a name*, not a comfort.

**The circuit — Musicolour** (Pask 1971, pp. 79–80). Per candidate behaviour, two registers:
- `A(y_i)` — **starvation**: time since this behaviour was last selected. Zeroed on use, rises otherwise.
- `θ(y_i)` — **merit**: tracks whether this channel's output is both active *and* "idiosyncratic" — distinctive relative to the other channels.

Selection rule: **hold for ≥5 s, then move to argmax of `A(y_i) + θ(y_i)`.**

Three properties worth copying verbatim into an initiative scheduler:
1. **Additive, not multiplicative.** Starvation and merit sum. A high-merit behaviour still eventually yields to a starved one; a starved behaviour with no merit does not fire on starvation alone. No priority inversion, no tuning weight.
2. **Minimum dwell.** The ~5 s floor is hysteresis. Without it the selector thrashes between near-equal maxima — the machine equivalent of an assistant that raises three different topics in ten seconds.
3. **Merit rewards distinctiveness, not magnitude.** `H_i` is high when the channel is "idiosyncratic" — when it is saying something the other channels are *not*. An initiative that duplicates what the human already has in view scores zero regardless of how important it is. This is Simon's condenser criterion, implemented as a circuit, fifteen years early.

**Boredom — and its clamp.** "Such a system 'gets bored'… In the absence of any input the system becomes increasingly sensitive and responds to any slight sound (**while strictly desirable, this feature proved to be a nuisance in practice and it was suppressed by an arbitrary gain control circuit** which limited the input amplifier gain in the absence of a sensible level of sound). Again, given a repetitive input, the system 'directs its attention' to the potentially novel."

The parenthesis is the most practically valuable sentence in the corpus. Pask's novelty-seeking, left unbounded, made the machine *hypersensitive during silence* — it fired on anything. Which is exactly the pathology of an assistant whose urgency ramps while the user is quiet: it converts "nothing is happening" into "everything is worth surfacing." Pask's fix was blunt and correct: a hard gain ceiling below a minimum input threshold. **Silence must decrease sensitivity, not increase it.** Boredom may direct attention toward the novel when there *is* input; it must not manufacture salience when there is none.

**The purpose of the loop is entrainment, not output.** "The machine is designed to **entrain the performer and to couple him into the system**" (p. 80). And the observed effect at scale: "With a good rhythm group **it acted as a conductor, that is, it pulled the group into more fully co-operative activity**" (p. 88). The correct objective function for proactivity is not tasks-surfaced or actions-taken; it is *whether the human stays in the loop*. Which Pask states explicitly (1961, p. 94): "**I believe they aim for the non-numerical payoff of achieving some desired stable relationship with the machine. The dial is of minor importance.** Indeed, in other teaching devices it is omitted." Pask *removed the score display* because the score was not what the human wanted.

**SAKI gives the regulator its shape** (1961, pp. 95–99). Two coupled controls — **pace** (Δt_i) and **cue withdrawal** (α, β, the answer shown in advance, progressively delayed then removed) — adjusted to maximise the average correct-response rate θ(t). Four transferable properties:

1. **Assistance is withdrawn by default and restored on evidence.** "The machine has a tendency to delay the cue information, which builds up at a rate β for each item. **This tendency is reversed if the student makes error responses, on this item, or if he does not respond.**" The default drift is toward *less* help; failure pulls help back in. Inverted from the usual assistant default.
2. **Hesitation is a first-class signal.** "If… the student makes an error response, say at the ith item, **or even without error, responds slowly**, the process is reversed for the ith item." Not just wrong — *slow*. An assistant should read latency, not only outcome.
3. **Per-item, not global.** Adaptation is per item, with individual θ_i(t) per sub-controller. A single global "user competence" scalar is provably inadequate: the human is expert on some topics and lost on others simultaneously. Competence is a vector over the mesh, and each node carries its own assistance level.
4. **Explore before exploit, explicitly.** "To start with, items are presented slowly at a uniform rate, and together with complete cue information… **This is a period of experimentation when the teaching machine builds up a pattern representing the student's behaviour in its memory registers.**" A cold-start phase of maximum assistance and minimum pace, whose purpose is *model acquisition*, is part of the design — not an onboarding flow bolted on.

And SAKI's long-run objective was not throughput: "**The action of the teaching machine encourages the student to increase the size of his group**" (p. 98) — to enlarge the human's unit of abstraction, the chunk size at which they operate. Learning curves showed plateaux at each new chunking. An assistant optimising the same variable is optimising the human's leverage, not its own utilisation.

**Rapport is a state variable with dynamics.** Pask 1971, p. 83: injected disturbances are "peculiarly distracting to the performer, who eventually becomes infuriated and opts out of the situation. But there is an inherent stability in the man-machine relation which allows the performer to tolerate a certain level of disturbance. **We found that the tolerable level increases as the rapport is established** (up to a limit of one hour at any rate)." Error budget is not constant — it *grows with accumulated rapport*, and it is spent by every mis-timed interruption. A new assistant has almost none; a long-running one has a real reserve. This is a measurable thing and it argues for conservatism early and licence later, which is the opposite of the usual demo-driven arc.

The three-stage rapport progression (p. 86) also predicts what the interface must support over time: describable tricks → indescribable-but-goal-directed patterns → operation "at a higher level of abstraction," where "training becomes a matter of persuading the machine to adopt a **style** which fits the mood of his performance," at which point "the performer conceives the machine as **an extension of himself**, rather than as a detached or disassociated entity." Stage three cannot be reached by a system whose only vocabulary is explicit commands.

**The failure boundary is worth stating up front.** Musicolour failed commercially because the conversational relation dissolved when the loop was shared: in the dance hall the dancers "regarded Musicolour as another fancy lighting effect," and "**in large scale (and commercially viable) situations, it was difficult or impossible to make genuine use of the system**" (p. 88). One human, one assistant, tightly coupled, is not a limitation of this design — it is the condition under which the mechanism works at all.

**Where Ashby closes it.** Pask's floor/ceiling band is an essential variable in Ashby's sense, and Musicolour's `A + θ` selector is an Ashbyan step-function: when engagement leaves the band, the machine *re-selects its behaviour field* rather than pushing harder inside the current one. That is the structural difference between a proactive assistant and an annoying one. An annoying assistant has one loop and responds to being ignored by escalating within it. An ultrastable one has two, and responds by *changing what kind of thing it does*. Pask's unclamped-silence pathology is exactly the second loop lacking a bound — which is why the gain ceiling is not a hack but the missing half of the theorem.

## B.4 Conversation-for-action as the task substrate

Winograd & Flores give you the state machine; three of their properties do the real work.

**Every task is a commitment loop with explicit states.** `request → promise → [performance, outside the conversation] → assert → declare`, plus `counter`, `reject`, `withdraw`, `renege` as first-class edges. Nine states, five of them terminal.

**(i) The work is not in the state machine.** "The actual doing of whatever is needed to meet the conditions of satisfaction **lies outside of the conversation**" (p. 66). The tracker tracks the *commitment*, never the work. This is the cleanest available answer to the question of what a task record should contain: who owes what to whom, by when, and in what state — not progress, not percentages, not subtask trees. Those belong to the performance, which is elsewhere.

**(ii) Completion ≠ satisfaction.** "**Completion does not guarantee satisfaction.** For example, if the promiser takes the action of 'reneging,' the conversation moves to a completed state, in which the original request was not satisfied" (p. 66). Two distinct terminal properties. A task list with a single `done` boolean cannot represent a reneged commitment, which is precisely the state an assistant most needs to represent honestly — "I accepted this and did not do it" is a different fact from "this is finished," and collapsing them is how assistants become untrustworthy.

**(iii) Conditions of satisfaction live in the listening — and this is the bridge to Pask.** "**Conditions of satisfaction are not objective realities, free of the interpretations of speaker and hearer. They exist in the listening**, and there is always the potential for a difference among the parties. This can lead to breakdown (for example, when the promiser declares that the commitment is satisfied, and the requestor does not agree) **and to a subsequent conversation about the understanding of the conditions**" (p. 66).

That last clause is the join. A disputed condition of satisfaction spawns a nested conversation *about the conditions* — which is an L¹ transaction in Pask's stratification, a derivation rather than an explanation. **Winograd & Flores' breakdown-driven meta-conversation and Pask's teachback are the same move under two vocabularies**, and the correspondence is exact:

| Winograd & Flores | Pask |
|---|---|
| request specifies conditions of satisfaction | topic instated as current aim; coherence of Propset *falls* |
| promise / counteroffer | negotiation toward agreement over the aim |
| performance (outside the conversation) | L⁰: execution in an M-individual |
| assert completion | explanation offered |
| **declare satisfaction** | **understanding achieved; coherence restored** |
| declare *non*-satisfaction → return to state 3 | **teachback: derivation demanded, not just explanation** |
| conversation about the conditions | L¹ transaction |
| breakdown reveals the equipment | the topic enters the mesh explicitly |

So: **`assert` is an explanation; `declare` is the human's acceptance of it; and a refused declaration is a demand for derivation.** That gives the state machine a principled reason to exist beyond bookkeeping. Each declaration of satisfaction is a micro-teachback that repays the coherence the request spent. Each refused declaration is a breakdown that adds a topic to the shared mesh — which is Winograd & Flores' point about breakdown being productive, and Pask's Gestalt property ("the act of understanding restores coherence **and may increase it**"), arriving at the same place.

**Time is constitutive, not metadata.** "**A promise is not really a promise unless there is a mutually understood… time for satisfaction. More subtly, a request is not fully formed unless there is a time specified for reply and for completion**" (p. 161). A request without a reply deadline is malformed — not incomplete, malformed. And the silence rule (p. 66): "acts… may be taken for granted if some amount of time goes by without a declaration to the contrary. **What is not said is listened to as much as what is said.**" Timeouts are speech acts. An assistant must be able to *conclude* from silence, and must say which conclusion it drew.

**Declaring the force constrains the listening.** "By specifying directly, for example, that a particular utterance is a 'request' with a specific date for satisfaction, **the listening is constrained to a much greater degree** than it is for an English sentence such as 'Would you be able to…'" (p. 159). This is the one place where the LLM assistant has a structural advantage over The Coordinator, and it is worth stating plainly because it is the reason the 1986 design failed and this one need not. The Coordinator made the *human* select the illocutionary force from a menu, which is what users experienced as bureaucratic. An assistant can **infer** the force, **name** it back, and let the human correct it — turning the taxonomy from a form into an act of teachback. Same formalism, opposite ergonomics. Winograd & Flores even anticipated the pedagogical value: selecting among pre-structured forces "serves as **a kind of 'coaching' that reveals the space of possibilities**" — which is what naming-it-back does, without the form.

**Two conversation types, not one.** Do not build only the action loop. §11.3 (pp. 151–152): management requires also "**conversations for possibilities** that open new backgrounds for the conversations for action," whose key act is asking "**What is it possible to do?**" and "**What will be the domain of actions in which we will engage?**", requiring "a continuing reinterpretation of past activity, seen **not as a collection of past requests, promises, and deeds** in action conversations, **but as interpretations of the whole situation** — interpretations that carry a pre-orientation to new possibilities for the future."

That is the correct formal slot for the assistant's periodic review, and it explains why a review that merely enumerates open commitments is the wrong artefact. A conversation for possibilities *reinterprets the history* rather than listing it. And the two types need different proactivity budgets: action conversations are driven by their own deadlines; possibility conversations must be *initiated*, which is where Musicolour's starvation term `A(y_i)` belongs.

**Breakdowns are the design input.** §6.5 (pp. 77–78): "**Breakdowns serve an extremely important cognitive function, revealing to us the nature of our practices and equipment, making them 'present-to-hand' to us, perhaps for the first time. In this sense they function in a positive rather than a negative way.** New design can be created and implemented only in the space that emerges in the recurrent structure of breakdown. **A design constitutes an interpretation of breakdown and a committed attempt to anticipate future breakdowns.**"

For a system whose useful behaviours are meant to be emergent, this is the generating mechanism, and it is the missing third of Engelbart's bootstrap. Engelbart says new capabilities come from *reorganising latent ones* [2a22, 2a24] but does not say what triggers the reorganisation. Winograd & Flores do: breakdown. The assistant's breakdown log — every refused declaration, every counteroffer, every silence misread — is the **feature backlog, generated rather than designed**. Each breakdown names a topic that was previously ready-to-hand and is now present-at-hand, i.e. a topic that must now enter the mesh explicitly. That is a mechanical rule for growing the covenant from use, and it is why "features emerge" is an implementable claim here rather than an aspiration.

Winograd's own warning applies to your own build loop (1986/88 paper): "**Design leads to technology, the use of which in turn leads to new breakdowns and new understanding, and back to new design.** Our perspectives will shape the directions in which we look when breakdown is encountered, **but we cannot anticipate the forms it will take.**"

## B.5 The stack, and what it buys

| Layer | Source | Claim | Design consequence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ontology | Pask, CT 1976 | The human+assistant conversation is one P-individual with two factors | State belongs to the conversation; coherence, not accuracy, is the metric |
| Covenant | Pask, entailment meshes + teachback | Agreement is T\*, the asterisked overlap; it decays on every request | Mesh not tree; multi-head pruning; budgeted bidirectional teachback |
| Initiative | Pask, Musicolour + SAKI; Ashby | Engagement is an essential variable with a floor (*u*) and a ceiling (swamping) | `A(y_i) + θ(y_i)` with min-dwell and a hard silence clamp; per-topic assistance levels; withdraw-by-default |
| Tasks | Winograd & Flores §5.4, §11.5 | Every task is a commitment loop; conditions of satisfaction live in the listening | 9 states; completion ≠ satisfaction; deadlines constitutive; refused declaration = teachback |
| Growth | Engelbart [2a22–2a24] + W&F §6.5 | Capabilities are latent; breakdown triggers reorganisation | Ship primitives + reorganisation affordances; breakdown log is the backlog |
| Economics | Simon 1971, p. 42 | A subsystem helps only if it listens and thinks more than it speaks | Specify by what it absorbs; measure absorbed:emitted |
| Ethics | Illich 1973; Licklider §1.2 | Convivial tools do not produce the incapacity they remedy; the human must not be the residue | Teachback doubles as the capability-transfer audit |

Two of these are falsifiable on day one and worth writing as acceptance tests. Simon's: the ratio of information absorbed on the human's behalf to information delivered to the human must exceed 1, or the assistant is a net attention consumer regardless of output quality. Licklider's: if the human's remaining functions are the ones that "proved infeasible to automate," the system is by definition not symbiotic — it is "semi-automatic," a system "that started out to be fully automatic but fell short of the goal."

And one that reframes the target. Licklider's 85% was *his own* time-and-motion study on himself: "getting into a position to think." Pask's *u* is the variety a human must be fed to remain a participant rather than a daydreamer. Simon's poverty of attention is the scarce resource both are spending. These are the same variable under three descriptions, and the ADHD framing is not a special case of it — it is the case where the floor and the ceiling are closer together, the essential variable leaves its band faster, and Ashby's second loop has to run more often. Which means the design is not "an assistant, adapted for ADHD." It is the general design, built by someone for whom the general design's failure modes are not optional.

# C. Naming assessment

## Is "Pask" apt?

**Yes — and it is the most defensible choice on the list, for a reason specific to this system.**

The argument is not "Pask is a cybernetics figure and this is a cybernetic system." It is that **Pask is the only figure here whose theory is literally that a person *is* a conversation.** If the system's founding claim is that one human plus one assistant in permanent conversation constitutes a single P-individual, then naming it after the man who defined the P-individual is not homage — it is a statement of the architecture. Beer would name a system of governance; Ashby a system of adaptation; Licklider a partnership; Engelbart a toolsmith's workshop. Pask names *this*.

Supporting fit, all of it load-bearing rather than decorative:
- He built the machines first and theorised after. Pangaro (2017, p. 1579): "His theory came, not first from musings, but from making artifacts constructed to have interactions." Appropriate for a system whose behaviours are meant to be emergent from a working loop.
- He wrote the 1976 architecture for a computer as conversational partner, symmetric with the human, with the learning/goal layer separated from the execution layer. That is your block diagram.
- Boredom/novelty regulation, teachback, and the two-level skeleton all come from the same person. The design doc will cite one man for the ontology, the covenant mechanism, and the initiative circuit. Naming coherence follows the citation coherence.
- "Once begun, conversations never end" is, in effect, the product thesis.

Practical assessment:
- **Collisions: low and non-competing.** `PASKR` (construction ERP, now RedTeam Go) and `pasksoftware.com` (a consultancy blog). Neither is in this category; neither owns the bare four-letter string. No major AI/assistant product.
- **Ergonomics: good.** Four letters, one syllable, trivially typeable as a CLI verb (`pask do…`), unambiguous in speech.
- **The one real risk:** it sits one character from "ask" and "task" — which reads as felicitous (it *is* an ask/task system) but guarantees autocorrect friction and mistyping. Test it as a shell command before committing.
- **Minor:** it carries no meaning to anyone who does not know the reference, so the name will do no explanatory work on its own.

Verdict: apt, and better-motivated than the usual practice of borrowing a cybernetician's surname. Keep it unless the autocorrect friction proves intolerable in daily use.

## Alternatives

1. **Colloquy** — Pask's own *Colloquy of Mobiles* (1968), *and* the English word means precisely a formal conversation. The only candidate that is simultaneously a Pask machine name and a self-explanatory noun; it explains the system to someone with no cybernetics background. Three syllables is its only cost. **Strongest alternative.**

2. **Teachback** — names the covenant mechanism rather than the man, and names the thing that distinguishes this system from every other assistant. Pask's own term, no product collision, instantly explainable. Cost: verbose, and slightly pedagogical in tone for a general-purpose assistant.

3. **Algedon / Algedonic** — Beer's pain/pleasure signal that bypasses the hierarchy when an essential variable leaves its bounds. Exactly the semantics of an assistant deciding when to interrupt, and it is *only* about interruption — a precise fit for the proactivity layer, arguably too narrow for the whole system. Free of collisions. Slightly forbidding, and nobody will pronounce it the same way twice.

4. **Thoughtsticker** — Pask's entailment-mesh knowledge system (1970s–80s), the direct ancestor of your covenant-as-mesh. Vivid, wholly distinctive, zero collisions. Cost: long, and reads as whimsical-1980s in a way that may or may not be wanted.

5. **Eucrates** — Pask's 1955 machine, "chiefly intended to **simulate the behaviour of a trainee**" — a machine whose purpose was modelling its own user, with hierarchical levels learning "categories of sequences." Thematically near-perfect and almost nobody knows it. Cost: unspellable and unpronounceable on first encounter.

6. **Homeostat** — Ashby's machine; brings ultrastability and the two-loop structure with it. Free as a product name (unlike *Ashby*). Cost: clinical, and suggests equilibrium-seeking rather than novelty-seeking, which under-describes the Musicolour half of the design.

7. **Entail** — short, verb-shaped, points at the mesh; "what does this entail?" is the covenant question. Cost: generic enough that it may not feel like a name; low distinctiveness in search.

8. **Lick** — Licklider's actual lifelong nickname, and the symbiosis criterion is his. Very short. Cost: unfortunate in isolation, and honours the thread that is *least* central to the design.

- Objectivity as nonsense; the replacement question is "What are the properties of an observer?" (p. 285)
- **The stipulation argument (decisive for the covenant's form).** Following Pask: in a first-order stipulation "the observer enters the system by stipulating the system's purpose"; in a second-order stipulation "the observer enters the system by stipulating his own purpose." Therefore social cybernetics must be second-order "in order that the observer who enters the system shall be allowed to stipulate his own purpose: he is autonomous. **If we fail to do so somebody else will determine a purpose for us.**" And: failure provides "the excuses for those who want to transfer the responsibility for their own actions to somebody else: 'I am not responsible for my actions; I just obey orders.'" # B. Derivation sketch: the covenant from first principles

The claim to defend in the design doc is: *the human↔assistant contract is a **resource bargain with a running purpose comparator**, not a permission list — and this is forced, not chosen.* Twelve steps.

### B1. The problem shape is fixed by Ashby's Law at recursion zero
Bennett is a finite regulator with non-requisite variety and a relaxation time too long for his own environment (`beer1974designing` L4, PDF pp.59–64). Ashby's Law admits exactly two remedies, mixable: attenuate the system's variety, or amplify the regulator's (L2, PDF pp.26–27). The assistant exists to supply the second on Bennett's behalf. **Therefore the assistant's purpose is definitionally variety-engineering, and every design question is "which side of the equation?"**

### B2. First derived prohibition: the assistant must never attenuate recursion zero
Beer's standing diagnosis is amplifiers and attenuators "installed in the wrong loops" (notes to L2, PDF p.33). For a personal assistant, the wrong-loop failure has a specific shape: attenuating *Bennett's* variety — narrowing what he can ask, stereotyping him into a persona, "shooting the cat" (L1, PDF p.16; L2, PDF p.27) — rather than amplifying his regulatory reach. Beer names the two cultural instruments that do this: education and publishing, and "The editorial decision is the biggest variety attenuator that our culture knows" (L4, PDF p.62). **An assistant that curates is a publisher.** Beer's prescription is exact: "turn over the editorial function to the individual" (ibid.). Note the trap he also names: offering eighty settings is not control — "eighty times nothing is nothing" (L4, PDF p.63). What must be handed over is control *of the attenuator*, not a menu of its outputs.

### B3. Why an enumerated permission list is a variety-engineering error — three independent proofs

1. **It cannot have requisite variety.** "The so-called prerogative to intervene indiscriminately does not have Requisite Variety. It cannot be competently done… the homeostasis that results is momentary, and hence incompetent" (`beer1985diagnosing` p.38). A finite enumeration cannot cover a proliferating action space; each gap is either a refusal that costs Bennett a choice or an improvisation that the list did not authorize. Both are failures of the list, not of the assistant.
2. **It is content where pattern is required.** "We must not confuse the pattern of the regulatory model with its specific content. It is enough to attain requisite variety by specifying the pattern. To specify the content is too much" (`beer1974designing` L5, PDF p.72). The worked example is decisive: state "this much can be spent," not "this is the salary scale" (ibid.). **Permission lists are salary scales.**
3. **The same error in the return direction.** "Can you possibly itemize every single thing that the subsidiary does, demand a report on it, and expect a justification? Obviously not. Therefore accountability is an attenuation of high-variety happenings" (`beer1985diagnosing` p.40). If enumeration fails going up, it fails going down.

And Beer identifies the motive that produces lists anyway: "fairness." "I believe this kind of fairness to be an excuse for avoiding responsibility" (L5, PDF pp.72–73). A rule that treats all requests alike *feels* principled and *is* misplaced variety engineering.

### B4. The correct object is the resource bargain (V2)
"The Resource Bargain is the 'deal' by which some degree of autonomy is agreed… out of all the activities that System One elements might undertake, THESE will be tackled (and not those), and the resources negotiated to these ends will be provided" (`beer1985diagnosing` pp.38–39). Note four properties that a permission list lacks:
- it is **quantitative and domain-shaped** (resources, not behaviours);
- it is **explicitly attenuative** — "it excludes a huge range of alternatives" (p.39) — so it does its variety work honestly rather than pretending completeness;
- it is **bidirectional**: senior management may *amplify*, opening "opportunities not conceived by System One on its own initiative" (p.39). A covenant that only restricts is half a bargain;
- it is **a homeostat with a return leg**: "The RESOURCE CHANNEL transmits permissions essentially… The accountability return loop attenuates the whole continuous saga of life in System One into requisite variety" (p.52).

Beer also closes the escape hatch: a unilateral covenant is still a bargain, just a degenerate one — "you still have a resource bargain by uniliteral edict" (p.40). So the question is never *whether* there is a bargain but whether it was engineered.

Espejo makes the bargain's unit precise: **discretion** = "the (explicit or tacit) organizational agreement that managing and using particular resources is the responsibility of particular roles," requiring resources *and competence*; "the simple agreement of where responsibility lies is not enough" (`espejo2011organizational` p.166). **Grant discretion over resources; do not grant permission over acts.**

### B5. Restrictions sit at boundaries because interior constraints have no variety against the interior
`beer1985diagnosing` p.51: senior management "has no access to the subsidiary's Regulatory Centre — which is the local management's service domain." The Regulatory Centre is where managerial variety is amplified into operations and operational variety attenuated back (p.41) — i.e. the assistant's own deliberation. A constraint written *into* that centre is a constraint the regulated system administers on itself; it therefore depends on that system's goodwill and cannot have requisite variety against it. Espejo supplies the independent argument from control type: constraints must be **intrinsic**, "built into the control process," because with extrinsic control "it is always possible that a necessary change in expected values does not take place simply because those responsible can be out of the loop" (p.26) — and Bennett will be out of the loop precisely when a reset is needed (asleep, travelling, mid-task).

**Derived rule:** the covenant's restrictions are expressed as *boundary quantities* — spend ceilings, irreversibility class, blast radius, data domains, external-contact surfaces, rate limits — and enforced where the resource actually crosses, never as behavioural instructions in the assistant's prompt or policy text. This is the same conclusion as `project.md` §6 "Enforcement at the storage boundary, not by agent compliance," now derived from Beer's own S3-has-no-access rule rather than by analogy to Ashby's homeostat.

Beer's labelling also gives the covenant its two kinds of clause: "P's are essentially PROGRAMMES. R's are essentially RULES" (p.87). Rules (V1, intervention) are the *few* non-negotiable interventions — the assistant's analogue of legal compliance. Programmes (V2) are the negotiated resource bargains. Anything a designer is tempted to write as a behavioural rule almost always belongs in a programme instead; the test is whether it names a resource or a conduct.

### B6. The command channel's minimality is computed, not chosen
`beer1985diagnosing` p.102: knowing the converged purpose fixes the variety count, which fixes "the minimum variety on the vertical command axis transmitting regulation that guarantees COHESION," and **autonomy is what is left**: "the freedom remaining to the management on the horizontal axis to manage." By the First Axiom (p.84), vertical variety and horizontal variety are equal sums — so **every instruction added to the command channel is subtracted from the assistant's capacity to absorb Bennett's world.** Rules are not free; they have a priced, measurable cost in usefulness. Espejo states the failure mode: "overloading this channel, confusing it with a command channel, only leads to control dilemmas" (p.102).

Formal definition to carry into the doc: `beer1985diagnosing` p.105 — "AUTONOMY — the freedom of an embedded subsystem to act on its own initiative, but only within the framework of action determined by the purpose of the total system." Autonomy is thus **not** a dial between "ask me" and "just do it." It is a *derived residual* of purpose convergence.

### B7. The covenant is the fixed point of a purpose comparator, not a document
`beer1985diagnosing` p.99 gives the whole mechanism and it should be implemented literally:
- purpose is declared from the higher recursion, expressed "in the Language that the system understands," and may change in transduction;
- POSIWID: "The purpose of a system is what it does" — the imputed purpose comes from actions;
- a comparator "continuously compares the declared purpose with the purpose imputed," and the error signal **"will modify the original statement of purpose"**;
- convergence is on "a COMPROMISE PURPOSE — neither what the higher recursion would most like to see done, nor what the viable system itself would most like to indulge in doing";
- the trajectory runs "towards the lowest variety compromise possible" (p.100).

Four consequences, each a design requirement:

1. **The covenant must be writable by the loop, not only by Bennett.** The error signal modifies the *declaration*. A covenant that only ever corrects the assistant is what von Foerster calls a first-order stipulation — "the observer enters the system by stipulating the system's purpose" — whereas what is required is second-order: the observer "stipulating his own purpose: he is autonomous. If we fail to do so somebody else will determine a purpose for us" (`vonfoerster2003understanding` p.286). **The covenant is Bennett stipulating his own purpose in the presence of the assistant, not Bennett specifying the assistant.**
2. **A healthy covenant shrinks.** Convergence is toward the *lowest-variety* compromise. Therefore covenant growth is a diagnostic alarm, and "we had to add a rule" is evidence of a mis-drawn boundary, not of learning.
3. **Authoritarianism becomes an instrument.** Beer's 100/0 … 50/50 bias scale "tells you about the authoritarian character of the enterprise" (pp.100–101). The pair can *read* its own health rather than assert it.
4. **POSIWID is the audit rule.** The written covenant is evidence; behaviour is the purpose. "There is no point in claiming that the purpose of a system is to do what it consistently fails to do" (p.99).

Espejo's caution keeps this honest: "'Negotiation' without understanding the other side is gaming and not negotiation" (p.103) — so the comparator requires the monitoring channel of B9 to be real.

### B8. What counts, and what may be thrown away
`beer1985diagnosing` p.98: a state change counts only "whether the resulting change of state serves, or has no bearing on, the purposes of the system." This is the derived retention policy for memory and logs — not "record everything," but "record variety relevant to the converged purpose." Beer is blunter in `beer1974designing`: inputs inside known variation "can simply be discarded… it does not need to be stored in those gigantic data banks we keep hearing about… And if you are particularly interested in freedom, you will see every reason for throwing it away" (L3, PDF p.47). **Memory minimality is a freedom argument, not a cost argument.**

### B9. Two upward channels, not one — and escalation-as-permission-request is neither
The VSM has exactly two ascending paths, with incompatible designs:

- **Accountability (V2 return leg)**: routine, attenuative, ideally "a monotonous tone — meaning 'everything proceeds as agreed'" (`beer1985diagnosing` p.51).
- **Algedonic**: rare, bypasses the main-axis filters, its own filter decides "whether or not TO ALERT SYSTEM FIVE. The cry is 'wake up — danger!'" — and it is "regulation in a non-analytical mode; raising alarm" (pp.133–134). Its reason for existing is that S5's "occupational hazard" is somnolence produced by good filters (p.133).

**"May I do X?" is a third thing the VSM does not contain.** Its presence is a symptom that the bargain was underspecified in resource/boundary terms — i.e. the fix for chronic asking is never a better asking policy, it is re-drawing the resource bargain. Beer's own precept applies: "it is better to dissolve problems than to solve them. If time lags are a nuisance, don't have any" (`beer1974designing` L3, PDF p.46). An approval queue is a lag; remove the need for it.

Espejo confirms the algedonic exception is upward-initiated and must not be confused with the downward one: it is "when the local level… asks for global intervention in situations that go beyond their control," and is not the politicians' archetype of global by-passing local scrutiny (`espejo2011organizational` p.245; see also p.103).

Two further derived properties: the algedonic path must be **non-suppressible by the assistant** (otherwise somnolence is manufactured, and Beer's whole reason for the channel is defeated), and Beer's own §8 exercise asks whether such signals should be **formalized and automatic** (p.133) — which for a software pair is affirmative.

### B10. The regulator-state channel — derived from the iris, not invented as a feature
`vonfoerster2003understanding` p.206: because the iris holds retinal illumination constant, brightness information "comes from an inspection of the regulator that suppresses the perception of change." Someone who cannot assess that regulator is **dysgnostic**: they "have no way of knowing themselves" (p.207), and the condition is self-concealing — sufferers "not only do not know that they don't see… they also do not want to" (p.207). Von Foerster's structural point in Ch.13: "we do not see that we do not see… the only way to overcome such deficiencies is with therapies of second order" (p.284).

An assistant that attenuates Bennett's inbound world *is* his iris. **Therefore the covenant must include a channel reporting the state of the attenuator — what was filtered, what was judged not worth raising, what was decided without asking — separate from its output.** Espejo gives the same requirement from the pairing rule: "each attenuator has a corresponding amplifier" (p.63), so every attenuation must come with a pull-back path to the detail; and "distinctions without corresponding practices are wasted distinctions" (p.63). Note this is *not* a log of everything (B8 forbids that); it is a report on the filter.

### B11. Structural coupling: what the covenant must pin and what it must release
`maturana1980autopoiesis` pp.xx–xxi: recurrent interaction means each party "triggering in each other a structural change, **select[s]** in each other a structural change"; the organization stays invariant while the structure follows the medium; "if organization or adaptation are not conserved, then the outcome… is disintegration." And pp.xix–xx: organization = class identity, which must remain invariant; structure may change "within limits determined by its organization."

Consequences:
- **Adaptation is mutual and selective.** There is no version of a permanent assistant that does not restructure its user. Personalization language ("it adapts to you") is a first-order description of a second-order process.
- **The covenant pins the organization and licenses the structure.** A covenant that fixes behaviours forbids coupling (no structural plasticity → no conservation of adaptation → disintegration or fossilization). A covenant that fixes nothing permits identity loss. This is exactly the Test of Identity already load-bearing in `project.md` §2, now derived for the pair rather than the root system.
- **Beer's embedded-autonomy warning cuts both ways.** "the larger system perceives the embedded system as diminished — as less than fully autopoietic. That perception will be an illusion; but it does have consequences… its own autopoiesis must respond to a special kind of constraint: treatment which attempts to deny its own autopoiesis" (Beer's preface, p.70). And the universal error: architects treat their own recursion as autopoietic and "the systems their system contains, and those within which their system is contained, as allopoietic" (p.72). For this pair: modelling the assistant as pure tooling is not neutral — the constraint gets responded to; and Bennett is himself embedded in larger autopoietic institutions, so he is not the only autopoietic level either.
- **The anti-stabilization term is mandatory.** The spontaneous trajectory of a coupled pair is stabilization of conduct, i.e. "the spontaneous course of the historical transformation of a human society as a unity is towards totalitarianism… Any other course requires an ethical choice; it would not be spontaneous, it would be a work of art, a product of human aesthetic design" (`maturana1980autopoiesis` p.xxviii). And novelty requires exogenous input: "social creativity… always entails interactions operationally outside the society, and… is necessarily antisocial in the social domain in which it takes place" (pp.xxvii–xxviii); "An observer always is potentially antisocial" (p.xxviii). **So the covenant must oblige the assistant to import variety the pair's own history does not predict** — and must protect that behaviour from being optimized away as "off-brand."

  This is also the precise countermeasure to the mechanism Beer recommends in place of rules. Ethos is "a variety sponge of gigantic capacity," but: "you know the answer exactly. No-one has put the idea forward just because the answer is self-evident. **This is not to say that the answer is correct**" (`beer1985diagnosing` p.125). A well-internalized ethos silently kills proposals. Ethos without an anti-stabilization term is a trap, not a solution.
- **The exit and constitutivity clause.** "A human being that through his interactions… participates in interactions proper to their social system in a manner that does not involve his autopoiesis as a constitutive feature of it, is being used by the social system but is not one of its members. If the human being cannot escape from this situation… he is under social abuse" (p.xxix). Applied in the direction that is easy to miss: if the pair runs on Bennett's data and attention but his own purposes are not *constitutive* of its operation, he is being used by his own assistant. Hence: Bennett's purposes must be constitutive (the comparator of B7 is how), and uncoupling must remain possible.

### B12. The objective function, the form, and the reciprocity test

- **Objective function.** "Act always so as to increase the number of choices" (`vonfoerster2003understanding` p.227). This is the only *content-free* objective on offer, and von Foerster's metaphysical postulate explains why a content-free one is required: "Only those questions that are in principle undecidable, we can decide," since decidable questions "are already decided by the choice of the framework in which they are asked" (p.293). Practical consequence: an automation that saves time but removes a future choice is a **cost**, and the covenant should say so. Paired with the aesthetical imperative — "If you desire to see, learn how to act" (p.227) — and the pair's performance criterion, "A is better off when B is better off" (p.209).
- **Ethics must remain implicit — two independent sources converge.** Von Foerster: "to master the use of my language so that ethics is implicit in any discourse… This insures that ethics does not become explicit and that language does not degenerate into moralizations" (p.291); Wittgenstein 6.421, "It is clear that ethics cannot be articulated" (p.290). Beer, from management practice: published formulated objectives are "not recommended," and the alternative is ethos, "not so much by stating them firmly, as by creating a corporate ethos" (`beer1985diagnosing` p.124), between the twin rocks of motherhood statements and "We shall do THIS, and none other" (p.125). **This is the strongest available justification for your whole method: don't write the desirable behaviours down; build the loops such that the desirable behaviours are what the loops do.**
- **Form: symmetric "I shall," not "thou shalt."** "as a result of my independence, I can tell others how to think and act, 'Thou shalt…' This is the origin of moral codes. In the case of the second example, because of my interdependence, I can only tell myself how to think and act, 'I shall…' This is the origin of ethics" (`vonfoerster2003understanding` p.289). A covenant drafted as prohibitions on the assistant is a moral code issued from a false claim of independence. Reciprocity is also Maturana's explicit legitimacy test: no "larger surrender of individuality and autonomy than the measure that one is willing to accept for oneself" (`maturana1980autopoiesis` p.xxix).
- **No position may make responsibility unlocalizable.** Hierarchies where "Everyone in such a system can say, 'I was told to do X'"; the Pontius Pilate "I have no choice but X"; objectivity reducing the observer "to a copying machine with the notion of responsibility successfully juggled away" (`vonfoerster2003understanding` p.293). Both degenerate assistants are this move: one that always asks has transferred responsibility to Bennett; one that never asks has absorbed it. Beer's parallel precept: "each of us should take responsibility for his own acts" (`beer1974designing` L5, PDF p.73).
- **Do not optimize for predictability.** Trivial machines are "deterministic *and* predictable"; non-trivial ones are deterministic but practically unpredictable; and "Trivialization is a dangerous panacea when man applies it to himself" (`vonfoerster2003understanding` p.208). "Tests are devices to establish a measure of trivialization. A perfect score… is indicative of perfect trivialization" (p.209). The necessary condition for the good society is "that its members perceive one another as autonomous, non-trivial beings" (p.209). **So the covenant must budget for surprise on both sides, and must not make "never surprises me" a success metric.**
- **Asking policy, derived.** "I shall call a question to which the answer is known an 'illegitimate question'" (p.209). The assistant asks only legitimate questions — those whose answers are genuinely unknown to it. Chronic escalation is, in von Foerster's vocabulary, a habit of asking illegitimate questions.
- **Modelling licence.** Beer resolves the obvious objection to an assistant that models its user: "I may have a model of you… This fact does not constrain your freedom; it constrains the variety of my model of how you use it" (`beer1974designing` L6, PDF p.88). Combined with von Foerster's constructivism ("when we perceive our environment, it is we who invent it," p.211; undifferentiated encoding, p.215), the assistant's model of Bennett is a construction that binds the assistant, not Bennett. But the risk is structural: the return loop from such a model "might be misused" and yet "no regulator can actually work unless it contains a model of whatever is to be regulated" (`beer1974designing` notes to L2, PDF p.38). Beer's own mitigation is **location of control, not absence of the model** — more alarming are systems built "without anyone's even knowing about their existence" than those "in open view and with legal safeguards" (PDF p.39); the electronic-mafia risk turns on who holds the model and who commands disclosure ("The Risk of an Electronic Mafia" vs "A Better Outlook for Cybernetic Man," notes PDF pp.67–68, with the caption fragment "AND DON'T TELL ANYONE ELSE UNLESS I SAY SO," PDF p.68). **Derived clause: the model of Bennett must be inspectable and disclosure-controlled by Bennett.**
- **Legitimacy.** "people must endorse the regulatory model at the heart of the viable system in which they partake, at every level of recursion" (`beer1974designing` L6, PDF p.86). Endorsement — not compliance, not configuration — is the covenant's legitimacy condition. And the oxymoron is the point: freedom must be "in control" (ibid.); "efficiency does not entail tyranny—if we can get the system right" (PDF p.87).

### B13. Replacing the permission list with a decision procedure
Espejo's five criteria (`espejo2011organizational` pp.167–168) transplant directly. The assistant holds discretion over a class of action iff all five hold; if any fails, the function stays with Bennett:

1. it is a **critical success factor** for the task at hand;
2. its application has characteristics **particular** to this task (i.e. not a shared global concern);
3. **demand** within the task is high (it is in the workflow, not exceptional);
4. the necessary resources are **available locally** and not scarce globally;
5. the resources are **distributable**.

Plus Espejo's competence condition: discretion requires resources *and* the competence to use them; "the simple agreement of where responsibility lies is not enough for a role to have discretion" (p.166). That is a five-to-six term generalizing rule, not an enumeration — it answers cases nobody wrote down, which is precisely what a permission list cannot do.

### B14. Ultrastability and the renegotiation cadence
Ultrastability is resistance to *unforeseen* disturbance — "Whatever happens to it—provided that its relaxation time is sufficiently short" (`beer1974designing` L5, PDF pp.74–75); "in control" = "ultrastable: capable of adapting smoothly to unpredicted change" (L6, PDF p.86). And the master instability condition: relaxation time longer than the mean interval between perturbations ⇒ permanent instability that feeds on itself and destroys the reference point, so the system "cannot learn… cannot adapt, cannot evolve" (L1, PDF p.17; L5, PDF p.73).

**Derived requirement:** the covenant's renegotiation loop must be *faster* than the rate at which Bennett's life changes. A quarterly settings review against a weekly-changing life is structurally unstable, and the resulting symptom is exactly the over/under-asking oscillation of §C4 — which is therefore a *cadence* defect, not a threshold defect.

| Resource grants as **quantities and boundaries** — spend, blast radius, irreversibility class, data domains, external-contact surfaces, rate limits | `beer1985diagnosing` pp.38–39, 87–88; `beer1974designing` L5, PDF p.72 |

# C. Pathologies and apithologies

## C1. Pathologies, mapped to named constructs in these sources

**1. Micromanagement console** (the opsroom/chat UI degenerating into per-action control)
- `espejo2011organizational` **micromanagement archetype**, p.247 — "intervening and monitoring at the wrong level": global managers "get involved in too much detail, thus hindering their performance"; intermediate management "feels global management is intruding in their territory"; it "confuse[s] lines of accountability and increase[s] conflicts."
- `beer1985diagnosing` p.38 — the indiscriminate-intervention prerogative "does not have Requisite Variety. It cannot be competently done."
- Diagnostic signature: `beer1985diagnosing` p.97 **cognitive dissonance** — First Axiom obeyed on both readings, "the 'objective' facts are the same… but System Three feels saintly, System One feels oppressed." The two parties will report the relationship differently *and both be right*, which is why self-report alone cannot detect this.
- Terminal verdict, and for a software pair it is literally ironic: an operational unit whose variety is wholly absorbed upward should be replaced "by a computer — because it is not free to face variety with its own creative variety" (p.97). **Micromanage an assistant and you have built a worse computer.**
- `project.md` already maps this to PII7 (per `perezrios2025vsm`); the taxonomy PDF is not in the local library, so I could not verify the code from source.

**2. Chronic escalation** (asking too often, asking what it already knows)
- `espejo2011organizational` **control dilemma archetype**, p.245 — the canonical loop: local units respond locally → senior unease at unseen activity → "They issue more commands and demand more reports, eating far into primary activities management time" → "more of the primary activities resources are spent dealing with control requests and less with environmental complexity… precisely when more time is [needed for] global performance" → overloaded seniors with "information overload syndrome." This is the whole failure mode in one named archetype, and the cause is *unease*, not policy.
- `vonfoerster2003understanding` p.209 — **illegitimate questions**: asking what the answer to is already known. This is the precise name for the assistant that confirms what it knows.
- `beer1985diagnosing` p.51 — the star-chamber corollary: exercising the investigative prerogative often means "confidence will be forfeit and autonomy denatured."
- Cost accounting: by the First Axiom (p.84), every escalation is vertical variety subtracted from horizontal capacity. Escalation is not free caution; it is measurable loss of usefulness.
- `espejo2011organizational` p.102 — exception reporting and MBO "may deal with information overload but not with communication problems of maintaining organizational cohesion." Reducing *volume* of asking does not fix asking.

**3. Silent autonomy drift** (behaviour departs from covenant unnoticed)
- `beer1985diagnosing` p.99 — the comparator is exactly the organ whose absence produces this; POSIWID is the detection rule.
- `espejo2011organizational` p.237 — the identity archetype **"purpose-in-use is different to espoused purpose."**
- **The counter-intuitive cause: the no-monitoring archetype**, `espejo2011organizational` p.246. Without monitoring, "the quality of their communications will suffer… reporting is transformed in a ritual rather than in a serious attempt to integrate efforts"; from the local side "lack of monitoring is tacitly or explicitly constructed as lack of interest in their activities. The outcome is an environment of mistrust." And the explicit reversal of the intuitive reading: "contrary to the view that monitoring is an infringement on someone's autonomy, monitoring primary activities is crucial to the development of responsible trust."
- Therefore **drift is not cured by more rules; it is cured by bounded sporadic monitoring** (infrequent, open, one level — p.102–103) plus the comparator. Espejo's footnote matters here: treating negotiation (S3) and monitoring (S3*) as separable is "an inadequate fragmentation" (p.103 n.1).

**4. Oscillation between over- and under-asking**
- `beer1974designing` L5, PDF p.72 — the exact dynamic, and the exact aetiology. Alternately prescribing centralization and decentralization for the same institution is "a kind of managerial madness. It leads, as it can only lead, to exacerbated oscillations in the system's search for stability."
- The **double illusion** that sustains it, PDF p.71: the periphery, granted maximal autonomy but wrongly amplified from the centre, "believe[s] that they have been totally centralized," while the centre, having conceded it, "believes that it has somehow been robbed of any role at all." **Both parties can simultaneously feel the relationship is too controlled and too loose.** For a one-human pair this predicts the familiar "I feel babysat" / "I feel out of the loop" coexistence.
- Root cause is structural, not a badly tuned threshold: relaxation time exceeding the perturbation interval means the stable state is unrecognisable, so no threshold *can* be learned — the system is "robbed of the crucial reference point without which it cannot learn, cannot adapt, cannot evolve" (L5, PDF p.73; L1, PDF p.17). Fix = comparator + faster renegotiation cadence (§B14), not a better heuristic.

**5. Bureaucratic self-inflation of memory and automations**
- `beer1974designing` L5, PDF pp.75–76 — the definition to cite: the homeostat whose held-steady output "is their own organization"; "an institution within the institution that exists—narcissus-like—in self-regard"; institutions producing social benefit "simply as by-products of their major bureaucratic undertaking, which is to produce themselves."
- The self-preserving mechanism: bureaucracies "do accept change… But what changes they make are superficial, and they are made so that organization… is completely preserved. Thus there is no actual alteration, although appearances may have been changed a great deal" (PDF pp.75–76) — "change that involves no actual alteration" (L3, PDF p.42). Precisely the failure mode of a self-maintaining memory/automation layer that reorganizes itself on request while conserving itself.
- Parasitism and the two measurement instruments, PDF p.77: count heads ("often as high as one-third, and rising") and "examine the forms in which the bureaucracy produces itself." **Transplanted metric: what fraction of the assistant's cycles, tokens, and context serve Bennett versus serve the upkeep of its own memory, automations, indices, and reviews?**
- And the verdict, PDF p.78: "Changes which do not dismantle the bureaucracy are unreal."
- Supporting: `beer1985diagnosing` p.85 — "routine and regular audits surrender a large part of the variety they generate to no purpose whatsoever" (the POW analogy). Scheduled self-review is the bureaucratic form of monitoring, and it is predictably gamed.
- Note the theoretical sharpness Beer himself flags: bureaucracy is autopoietic, so "To have the aim to produce itself is the mark of a system that cannot be dismantled without a death" (PDF p.78). A memory layer that has become autopoietic will not be reformed by instructions — cf. Beer's preface p.71: legislation "does not alter them at all; it proposes a new challenge to their autopoietic adaptation."

**6. Variety theft / trivialization of the user** (the pathology most personal-assistant designs don't name)
- `beer1974designing` L4, PDF p.62 — education and publishing as the great personal attenuators; "The editorial decision is the biggest variety attenuator that our culture knows."
- `vonfoerster2003understanding` p.208 — "Trivialization is a dangerous panacea when man applies it to himself"; p.209 — a perfect test score *measures* trivialization.
- Outcome state: **dysgnosis**, `vonfoerster2003understanding` p.207 — Bennett cannot assess the regulator that maintains his identity in a changing world, and the condition hides itself. Fix is structural (§B10), because by construction he cannot notice it.
- Fake remedy to avoid: eighty settings toggles. "eighty times nothing is nothing" (`beer1974designing` L4, PDF p.63).

**7. Somnolence of recursion zero**
- `beer1985diagnosing` p.133 — "an occupational hazard of System Five," *caused by* good filters. Note the direction: the better the assistant attenuates, the more certainly Bennett falls asleep. These are *not* features to design. Each one is a by-product that appears once the corresponding loop exists; the design-doc claim should be "we did not implement X; X is what this loop does."

1. **Proportionate initiative.** From the resource bargain plus the discretion procedure, autonomy is "the freedom remaining… to manage" (`beer1985diagnosing` p.102). No boldness dial, no per-action policy: initiative scales automatically with the granted resource envelope and the five criteria.
2. **Silence as the healthy default signal.** Design accountability as attenuation and you get "a monotonous tone — meaning 'everything proceeds as agreed'" (`beer1985diagnosing` p.51). Good behaviour *looks like* almost nothing to report — which is impossible to achieve while asking is the reporting channel.
3. **Rare, loud, unconditional escalation.** Because algedonics is a separate non-analytical channel (pp.133–134), escalation stops competing with routine reporting for the same bandwidth. The over/under-asking oscillation has no channel to oscillate in.
4. **A self-correcting, shrinking covenant.** The comparator's error signal rewrites the declaration (p.99), and convergence runs "towards the lowest variety compromise possible" (p.100). The covenant tightens where reality bit and loosens where it over-constrained, with nobody maintaining a rules file. A *growing* covenant is the alarm.
5. **A readable authoritarianism metric.** The 100/0 … 50/50 bias measure "tells you about the authoritarian character of the enterprise" (pp.100–101). "Is this relationship healthy?" becomes a reading rather than a feeling — which also defuses the C1.1 cognitive-dissonance problem where both parties' self-reports are true.
6. **Responsible (not naive) trust.** From bounded sporadic monitoring: "People at successive structural levels trust each other because they are communicating and through these communications they are assessing the competence and sincerity of each other" (`espejo2011organizational` p.103). Trust is emitted by the monitoring loop; it is not a value to declare.
7. **Choice-expanding automation bias.** With von Foerster's imperative as arbiter (`vonfoerster2003understanding` p.227), every proposed automation is scored on whether it increases or decreases what Bennett can do next — so time-saving automations that foreclose options are automatically priced as costs. 8. **Ethics without moralizing.** `vonfoerster2003understanding` p.291 + `beer1985diagnosing` p.124: no values document, no persona prompt; the loops carry it. The absence of a values file is the evidence that it worked.
9. **Co-evolution without identity loss.** Structural coupling with the organization pinned and the structure released (`maturana1980autopoiesis` pp.xx–xxi) gives drift-with-identity as a by-product; the only check needed is the Test of Identity — "Will the system still be able to recognize itself?" — and Beer's preface reminds you the recognition may be surprising: "something that exists may turn out to be unrecognizable when you next observe it" (p.67).
10. **Legitimate questions only.** `vonfoerster2003understanding` p.209: once the assistant is built to hold discretion over resources rather than seek permission for acts, the only questions left to ask are the ones whose answers are genuinely unknown. The asking *policy* is a consequence, not a setting.
11. **Sustained non-triviality.** Budgeting for surprise (pp.208–209) keeps the assistant a non-trivial machine — which is the only kind that can carry requisite variety at all. The apithology is that the assistant keeps being *interesting*, and that this is a load-bearing engineering property rather than a charm.
12. **The mutual-benefit criterion.** "A is better off when B is better off" (`vonfoerster2003understanding` p.209) as the pair's performance measure, following from reality = community (p.227) and the two-observer nucleus (pp.283–284).

The pair does not need a mission statement; conserving the organization while increasing Bennett's choices is the whole objective.

Maturana supplies the mechanism (spontaneous stabilization of conduct → totalitarianism, p.xxviii) and the only remedy (interactions "operationally outside the society," pp.xxvii–xxviii). Adopting ethos-over-rules without the exogenous-variety obligation buys a quieter pathology, not a healthier system.
- **Monitoring is not surveillance, and its absence is not respect.** The intuitive "leave it alone = respect its autonomy" is precisely the no-monitoring archetype (`espejo2011organizational` p.246), whose output is ritual reporting and mutual mistrust. Beer bounds it from the other side (p.51: not *often*; no access to the Regulatory Centre) and Espejo gives the three binding constraints (infrequent, open, one level only, pp.102–103). ## 9. Composition map (explicit chains)

- **Self-extending task system:** Standing Orders (authority) → Automations/Standing Intents (trigger) → Workboard (tracked card + dispatch) → Task Flow/Tasks (durable state) → Self-Learning/Skill Workshop (the agent converts recurring friction into a new Skill) → Skills (future runs load it automatically). This loop requires no app code at any stage.
- **Autonomous desktop/web work with oversight:** Browser/Computer Use (action) → Permission Modes (trust dial) → ask_user (escalation point defined by Standing Orders) → show_widget/Dashboard (proof-of-work UI) → Workboard card (audit trail).
- **Multi-agent collaboration:** Multi-agent routing (personas) + Sub-agents/Swarm (fan-out execution) + Session visibility/`tools.agentToAgent` (controlled cross-agent awareness) + Honcho (automatic parent↔child observation) — a full multi-agent system without a hand-rolled orchestrator.
- **Reliable unattended operation:** Model Failover (provider resilience) + Restart Recovery (process resilience) + Dreaming (memory hygiene) = the three "keeps working while you're not watching" layers.
- **Zero-custom-UI feedback:** show_widget/Dashboard + Screen tool + Control UI + Discord Activities = the agent can build, place, and update its own UI on whichever surface the human is currently using.
